strengths: Strong empirical results with >22% MAE improvement on REC-8K and consistent gains across multiple datasets (REC-8K, FSC-147, CARPK)
Valuable practical insight identifying object-centric detection (centroids vs bounding boxes) as key for counting tasks, with potential applicability beyond REC
Comprehensive and rigorous experimental evaluation including thorough ablation studies (Tables 4-6), analysis across object count ranges, and qualitative results with failure case analysis

Well-motivated approach with clear problem formulation: using contrastive learning in image space to distinguish visually similar objects with different referring expressions, avoiding image-text misalignment issues
Good presentation quality with effective use of visualizations, clear method description, implementation details provided, and proper attribution with comprehensive related work
Demonstrated versatility by successfully adapting the framework to class-agnostic counting tasks
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core contribution is primarily applying supervised contrastive learning with a straightforward modification to filter negatives (Equations 4-5), rather than introducing fundamentally new techniques

Insufficient analysis of why and how contrastive learning helps: paper shows improvements but provides limited insight into what discriminative features are learned or why alternatives fail. Ablation in Table 6 suggests the strong baseline contributes significantly but this is not clearly disentangled from CL contributions
Design choices lack justification: the 0.50 LCLS threshold appears arbitrary without ablation studies or sensitivity analysis; selection strategy for positive samples needs more detailed description
Modest improvements on class-agnostic counting tasks (FSC-147: 0.19 MAE improvement on CARPK) limiting claimed generality; strongest results are specific to REC domain
Missing computational cost analysis: no discussion of training time, memory requirements, or inference speed compared to baselines, which is important for practical adoption
Limited failure mode analysis in main paper: while supplementary material includes some examples, systematic analysis of when/why the method fails is minimal

Incomplete experimental details: unclear how ground truth object counts are used during training for positive class masking; lack of sensitivity analysis on hyperparameters and statistical significance testing (no error bars or confidence intervals across multiple runs)

Evaluation concerns for class-agnostic tasks: comparisons against methods with different supervisions (VE vs. Both visual exemplars and text) make fair comparison difficult; adaptation procedure for class-agnostic counting differs from REC without clear justification

strengths: Strong empirical results on REC-8K achieving state-of-the-art performance with >22% MAE improvement
Comprehensive experimental validation including multiple datasets, baselines, and ablation studies
Practical identification that object centroid-based detection outperforms bounding box and density-based methods
Versatility demonstrated through adaptation to class-agnostic counting tasks
Well-organized presentation with good qualitative examples showing both successes and failures
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily applies existing supervised contrastive learning to a detection framework with straightforward modifications

Unclear attribution of improvements: 'GDino improved' baseline already achieves 5.92 MAE; C-REX gain is modest (~1 MAE point), suggesting the detection-based approach, not contrastive learning, drives performance
Weak theoretical justification for the modified supervised contrastive loss (Eq. 4); no principled explanation for why using only positive anchors is superior
Incomplete ablation analysis that fails to isolate the contrastive learning contribution from other changes (detection baseline, loss reformulation, hyperparameters)
Limited evaluation scope: restricted to counting with fine-grained attributes; claims of generality not well-supported by class-agnostic counting results where improvements are less pronounced
Missing analysis of computational costs, failure modes, and hyperparameter sensitivity
Lack of statistical significance testing for reported improvements

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing an underexplored task (Referring Expression Counting) with clear practical importance for fine-grained visual understanding
Novel application of contrastive learning in image space rather than image-text space, cleverly avoiding misalignment issues inherent in text-image CL for this task
Strong experimental results with 22% improvement in MAE on REC-8K dataset over prior work, with consistent improvements across three different datasets (REC-8K, FSC-147, CARPK)
Comprehensive experimental validation including thorough ablation studies (Section 4.5) that validate design choices and demonstrate the importance of proposed modifications
Clear presentation with well-organized paper, informative figures (especially qualitative comparisons in Figure 2), and adequately described methodology
Solid detection-based baseline (Section 3.1) that is competitive even before contrastive learning, providing good foundation and reference point
Versatility demonstrated through successful extension to class-agnostic counting, showing generality beyond specific REC domain
weaknesses: Limited core technical novelty - primarily adapts existing techniques (Grounding DINO, supervised contrastive learning) to new task domain rather than introducing fundamentally new methods
Marginal improvements on secondary benchmarks (FSC-147: 10.19 vs 10.06; CARPK: 4.21 vs 3.80) suggest method may be overfitted to REC-8K characteristics

Insufficient mechanistic analysis of why contrastive learning specifically helps with referring expression counting - limited ablation on loss formulation and no visualization/analysis of learned representation space
Dataset scale concerns - REC-8K contains only 8,011 images, relatively small for modern deep learning; no discussion of annotation quality, reliability, or potential biases
Missing computational analysis - no evaluation of training time, memory requirements, or inference speed compared to baselines, important for practical adoption
Limited generalization testing - method not evaluated on unseen referring expression types; sensitivity to number of selections and positive/negative samples incompletely explored
Minimal failure mode analysis despite showing failures in supplementary material; limited discussion of when detection-based approach struggles or when contrastive learning doesn't provide benefits
Incomplete investigation of hyperparameter sensitivity - loss combines three weighted terms but sensitivity analysis for λ_cls, λ_sup, λ_pos is absent

strengths: Clear problem identification with well-motivated critique of image-text contrastive learning limitations (misalignment and limited negatives) for REC
Strong and consistent empirical results across three different REC architectures with improvements up to 28% MAE and 24.5% RMSE on REC-8K
Well-executed experimental validation with comprehensive ablations examining positive sample selection, loss modifications, and CL strategy comparisons
Practical contribution as a plug-in module applicable to multiple existing architectures without architectural changes
Thorough evaluation across multiple metrics, count ranges, and datasets with good qualitative analysis
Well-presented paper with effective visualizations clearly communicating the core idea
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: image-space contrastive learning is established in other domains (ReID, segmentation); the contribution is largely a straightforward application with a minor loss modification lacking strong theoretical justification

Severely limited generalization: minimal improvements on FSC-147 class-agnostic counting (margins <1-2% MAE) contradicts the claimed general applicability and suggests the method is specifically tuned to REC

Lack of deep analysis: no embedding space visualizations (t-SNE/UMAP) to verify claimed cluster compactness; insufficient investigation of why the modified loss is necessary; no sensitivity analysis for bipartite matching quality
Contradictory empirical evidence: Table 5a shows CAD-GD performs worse with C-REX on paraphrased expressions (MAE 6.85→8.02), directly contradicting robustness claims made in the paper

Insufficient theoretical grounding: the modified supervised contrastive loss (Eq. 2) lacks rigorous justification beyond intuition that negatives lack semantic coherence; efficiency claims rely on indirect CLIP vs DINOv2 comparisons rather than direct evidence

Experimental gaps: no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals; CAD-GD required retraining (no official checkpoint); dense scene analysis acknowledged but dismissed without quantitative evidence
Limited scope: improvements appear specific to REC formulation with minimal transfer value; frozen encoders limit improvement sources; relatively niche application domain

strengths: Clear motivation identifying genuine limitations of image-text contrastive learning for REC (limited negatives, poor alignment, instability)
Comprehensive experimental validation with consistent improvements across three architectures and two backbones on REC-8K
Well-designed ablation studies examining multiple components (image-text vs image-space CL, positive sample selection strategies, loss modifications)
Good presentation with clear visualizations and reproducibility details
Plug-and-play integration into existing architectures without modification
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: applies existing supervised contrastive learning [35] with a minor modification (optimizing only positives as anchors); image-space CL is well-established in vision tasks

Title and claims are oversold: 'What is the Right Embedding Space?' suggests a general principle, but the finding is task-specific to REC; claims about 'generality' not supported by weak class-agnostic counting results
Weak generalization beyond REC: FSC-147 shows minimal or negative improvements (GroundingREC regresses from 10.12 to 12.46 MAE); paraphrased RE robustness degrades for CAD-GD (6.85→8.02 MAE)

Insufficient mechanistic analysis: no embedding visualizations, no explanation of why combining image-text and image-space CL is harmful (Table 3), lacks interpretability about learned fine-grained distinctions

Critical dependence on bipartite matching for label assignment inadequately addressed: early training predictions are poor, creating potential negative feedback loop; no analysis of sensitivity or robustness to matching errors
Limited scope: only tested on REC-8K (8,011 images) and FSC-147; no cross-dataset evaluation or investigation of generalization to unseen referring expressions
The RE is still used for cross-attention conditioning—not truly 'visual-only' learning as claimed
Missing analysis of computational costs (bipartite matching overhead) and token count sensitivity

strengths: Strong and consistent empirical results with up to 28% improvement in MAE across multiple REC architectures (GroundingREC, CAD-GD, GroundingDINO)
Clear problem formulation: effectively identifies the limitations of image-text contrastive learning (poor alignment, limited negatives ~4 vs >100) and proposes a well-motivated solution

Comprehensive experimental validation including: proper ablation studies (Table 3-4), analysis across count ranges (Figure 4), extension to class-agnostic counting, robustness to paraphrasing, and comparison with VLMs
Practical and generalizable contribution: framework works as a simple plug-in module across different architectures without modification
Well-reasoned loss function modification (Eq. 2): using only positives as anchors is justified by the observation that negatives lack semantic coherence, validated by ablation
Excellent presentation with clear motivation, effective visualizations (especially Figures 1-2), and comprehensive supplementary materials including qualitative results and failure cases
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: applies established supervised contrastive learning techniques (used in ReID, segmentation) to a new domain; the core insight that image-space CL is preferable to image-text CL is relatively straightforward once the misalignment problem is identified

Insufficient analysis of scalability and failure modes: acknowledged concerns about dense scenes reducing negative pools are not thoroughly investigated; Figure 8 shows failures but lacks detailed analysis of when and why the method breaks down

Incomplete investigation of bipartite matching dependency: no sensitivity analysis to matching errors; alternative strategies mentioned but not comprehensively explored; computational cost not discussed
Lack of theoretical justification: no analysis of whether improvements stem purely from increased negative samples or from avoiding misalignment; unclear if the modified loss generalizes beyond REC
Limited dataset scope: primary evaluation on relatively small REC-8K (~8k images); class-agnostic results on single dataset (FSC-147); cross-dataset generalization not explored

Missing ablation studies: limited exploration of loss variants; no ablation on encoder freezing choices; no analysis of performance degradation as negative pool size decreases; lack of statistical significance testing
